Who do they answer to?

How to read the building

  1. Floors are the parts of the system, roof to foundation. Each names its question.
  2. Tiles are variables: a quantity or condition in the model that can rise or fall. Its definition states what a higher or lower value means.
  3. Arrows between floors count the connections that pass up. The heavy ones trace the main circuit.
  4. The return line at left carries policy’s effects back down to Wealth.
  5. Below the heavy ground line sit the economy and technology layers, on Newsprint.

Inside a floor, lines carry their evidence

  • Documented: on the public record
  • Plausible: some evidence
  • Contested: evidence disputed
  • Hypothesis: untested

The connected variables tend to move in the same direction, with the model's other conditions held steady. A positive sign does not mean a benefit.

Area C · Elections · Electoral competition

Safe seats move the deciding vote to the primary and lower the risk of losing office.

Who picks them? Whether officials can lose their seats, and who controls the rules of elections. Five variables share this floor; 20 connections touch them, and seven loops pass through.

The floor plan

The five rooms of Elections and the five connections between them. The safe-seat loop runs along the row and back underneath.

Point at, tap or tab to a room or a connection to read it.

The floor plan in words
  1. L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive. From C1 Safe seats to C2 Seats settled in the primary. Sign +, raises. Evidence documented. Delay under 2 years.
  2. L24: Electoral pressure leads to actual defeats. From C3 Risk of losing office to C5 Incumbents defeated. Sign +, raises. Evidence well supported. Delay 2 to 10 years.
  3. L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure. From C2 Seats settled in the primary to C3 Risk of losing office. Sign −, lowers. Evidence well supported. Delay under 2 years.
  4. L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats. From C4 Incumbents control election rules to C1 Safe seats. Sign +, raises. Evidence documented. Delay 2 to 10 years.
  5. L53: Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves. From C3 Risk of losing office to C4 Incumbents control election rules. Sign −, lowers. Evidence plausible. Delay 2 to 10 years.
  1. C1

    Safe seats

    Seats with little electoral competition

    Districts where one party wins by a wide margin, so its candidates face little risk in the general election. The model counts seats won by more than 10 percentage points.

    A higher value means more seats are safe for one party.

    Why it matters In a safe seat the November winner is close to certain, so the race that matters happens earlier.

  2. C2

    Seats settled in the primary

    How often the primary decides the winner

    The share of seats where the general election is so predictable that the primary settles who takes office. Turnout in that deciding contest can be far lower than in November.

    A higher value means more seats are settled in the primary.

    Why it matters A small, low-turnout primary electorate ends up choosing the representative for everyone.

  3. C3

    Risk of losing office

    Risk of losing office

    The credible threat that an incumbent will lose the next election. Where seats are competitive, the threat pushes officials to respond to voters before anyone is removed.

    A higher value means incumbents face a more credible chance of defeat.

    Why it matters The chance of losing is what makes officials listen. Without it, voters lose their strongest tool.

  4. C4

    Incumbents control election rules

    Officeholders' control over election rules

    The power of people already in office to set district maps, voting-access rules and local election choices. This is rule-setting authority, and each rule's effect needs its own evidence.

    A higher value means incumbents have more say over the rules of their own elections.

    Why it matters The people who benefit from today’s maps and voting rules are often the ones who write them.

  5. C5

    Incumbents defeated

    Incumbents defeated or pushed into retirement

    Officeholders who lose an election or retire under threat of defeat. This consequence is measured separately from the pressure they face while still in office.

    A higher value means more incumbents lose or retire under threat of defeat in an election cycle.

    Why it matters Defeats are how the system corrects itself. They show that poor performance has a cost.

The issues tracked here

39 active issue records touch these five variables. Open any one for its real-world problem, a fix tried somewhere, and what the evidence says.

Elections and representation 22

  • Registration hurdles and roll errors keep eligible people from votingIn the real world: Brooklyn voters wrongly dropped before a 2016 primaryWell supportedI017

    Eligible people can miss an election because registering is hard or because their record was wrongly removed from the rolls. The burden falls hardest on people who move often.

    The problem, in the real world

    Brooklyn voters wrongly dropped before a 2016 primary

    New York City's Board of Elections removed more than 117,000 Brooklyn voters from the rolls before the 2016 presidential primary. In a 2017 consent decree the board admitted it broke state and federal law. It agreed to review removals back to 2013 and restore voters it had wrongly purged.

    Brooklyn, New York City, New York · 2016 · Source: WNYC, City Board of Elections Admits It Broke the Law, Accepts Reforms, 2017

    A fix, in the real world

    Oregon registers voters automatically at the DMV

    Oregon began registering people automatically when they visited the Department of Motor Vehicles, under a 2015 law. More than 230,000 people were added through the program by the 2016 election, and 97,184 of them voted for president.

    Registration grew by more than 230,000, but about 43% of automatic registrants voted in 2016, compared with 79% of people who registered by mail or online.

    Oregon · 2016 · Source: Stateline (Pew Charitable Trusts), Oregon's First Test of Automatic Voter Registration Has Mixed Results, 2016

    How it works
    Registration hurdles and flawed maintenance of voter rolls keep some eligible people from voting, and the burden falls unevenly.
    Evidence
    Well supported. The Brennan Center for Justice, a voting-rights research and advocacy organization, counted about 16 million voters removed from rolls nationwide between 2014 and 2016, with removal rates rising in places formerly covered by federal preclearance after Shelby County v. Holder (2013). These are removal rates. The count does not show how many removals were mistakes.
    Response
    States, and Congress for federal elections, would adopt automatic and same-day registration, keep rolls accurate with secure methods, and give voters notice and a chance to correct their record before any removal.
    Who acts
    Congress for federal elections; states
    Tradeoff
    Rules must protect eligibility checks and data security, and keep noncitizens from being enrolled by mistake.
    Success looks like
    Share of eligible people registered, wrongful removals, and provisional ballots accepted.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-05 Automatic voter registration. Registers eligible people through routine dealings with state agencies, removing the registration step that falls hardest on people who move.
  • Long lines make voting cost more in some neighborhoodsIn the real world: Maricopa County cut polling places and lines stretched hoursWell supportedI018

    In some places voters wait far longer to cast a ballot, often because their polling places get fewer machines and staff. Waiting costs the most for people who cannot leave work.

    The problem, in the real world

    Maricopa County cut polling places and lines stretched hours

    Maricopa County, Arizona, opened 60 polling places for its March 2016 presidential primary, down from about 200 four years earlier. One Phoenix voter waited more than five hours, and some people were still in line at midnight. County Recorder Helen Purcell told supervisors she took full responsibility for the cut.

    Maricopa County, Arizona · 2016 · Source: Cronkite News (Arizona PBS), Phoenix Mayor Greg Stanton calls for Justice Department investigation of Maricopa County election debacle, 2016

    A fix, in the real world

    Georgia ties precinct size to hour-long lines

    Georgia's 2021 voting law requires action when voters wait more than an hour at an Election Day precinct. Officials must then cut the number of voters assigned there to no more than 2,000. Election Day lines have been rare in Georgia since the chaotic 2020 primary, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported in 2026.

    Average Election Day waits have run about two minutes since 2020, the newspaper reported, though no study isolates this rule's effect and some early-voting sites saw waits of 30 minutes or more in 2026.

    Georgia · 2021 to 2026 · Source: Atlanta Journal-Constitution, Georgia voters will see short lines and secure elections, Raffensperger says, 2026

    How it works
    Long lines and limited hours cost more for workers and for voters in minority precincts, where polling places often get fewer resources.
    Evidence
    Well supported. Using smartphone location data from the 2016 election, Chen, Haggag, Pope and Rohla (2019) found that residents of Black neighborhoods waited 29% longer to vote than residents of white neighborhoods; the measurement is strong and covers one election. Pettigrew (2017), working from surveys and observational data, found that minority voters wait longer and traced the gap to how local officials allocate precinct resources. A 2014 Government Accountability Office review of the 2012 election reported that some voters waited over an hour.
    Response
    States and local election offices would set service standards for polling-place access, early voting and mail voting, fund the staff needed to meet them and track the results.
    Who acts
    States; local election offices
    Tradeoff
    Costs and geography differ from place to place, and any expansion has to keep a secure chain of custody for ballots.
    Success looks like
    Wait times by precinct, and ballot rejection rates.
  • Voters with disabilities and limited English face barriers to voting on their ownIn the real world: Harris County polling places had barriers for disabled votersDocumentedI019

    Some voters with disabilities cannot cast a private ballot without help, and some voters who need language assistance do not receive it. Each voting method needs testing with the people who use it.

    The problem, in the real world

    Harris County polling places had barriers for disabled voters

    Harris County, Texas, had more than 750 polling places in 2019, the third-largest voting program in the country. The Justice Department alleged that many had barriers such as steep ramps and locked gates. A 2019 settlement required the county to survey nearly two-thirds of its sites and offer effective curbside voting.

    Harris County, Texas · 2019 · Source: U.S. Department of Justice, Justice Department Reaches Agreement with Harris County, Texas, to Ensure Polling Place Accessibility, 2019

    A fix, in the real world

    Ballots in voters' own languages raised participation

    The Voting Rights Act requires counties and towns with sizable language-minority populations to provide ballots and help in those languages. Studying 1,465 jurisdictions in the 2012 election, political scientists Bernard Fraga and Julie Lee Merseth compared places just above and just below the coverage cutoff.

    Coverage under the language provisions brought a significant increase in Latino registration and in Asian American turnout, the 2016 study found.

    U.S. counties and towns covered by the Voting Rights Act's language provisions · 2012 election (study published 2016) · Source: Fraga and Merseth, Journal of Race, Ethnicity, and Politics (Cambridge University Press), Examining the Causal Impact of the Voting Rights Act Language Minority Provisions, 2016

    How it works
    Voters with disabilities cannot reliably vote independently, and required language assistance does not always reach the voters who need it.
    Evidence
    Documented. The U.S. Election Assistance Commission's survey series found that the turnout gap between voters with and without disabilities fell from 16.8 points in 2000 to 11.3 points in 2020, with difficulties persisting. In a sample of 178 polling places in 2016, the Government Accountability Office found that 60% had at least one impediment to access.
    Response
    Election administrators would audit every voting method for disability access and provide the language assistance the law requires, testing each with the voters who use it. The Justice Department would enforce these duties.
    Who acts
    Election administrators; DOJ
    Tradeoff
    Accessible voting technology needs security protections and a backup method.
    Success looks like
    Voters with disabilities who vote independently and successfully, and accessibility complaints.
  • Conviction rules keep millions from votingIn the real world: Florida tied restored voting rights to paying court debtsDocumentedI020

    About 4 million Americans could not vote in 2024 because of a felony conviction, under rules that differ by state. Lifetime bans, confusing eligibility and payment conditions keep many excluded after release.

    The problem, in the real world

    Florida tied restored voting rights to paying court debts

    Florida voters restored voting rights to most people with felony convictions in 2018. The next year lawmakers required them to settle all fines and restitution first. In 2020 a federal appeals court upheld that rule 6-4, leaving people who cannot pay their court debts unable to vote.

    Florida · 2018 to 2020 · Source: Associated Press (via Boston Globe), Florida felons can't vote until they pay fines, fees, appeals court rules, 2020

    A fix, in the real world

    Minnesota restored the vote on release from prison

    Minnesota's 2023 law restores voting rights to people with felony convictions once they leave prison, instead of after probation ends. An estimated 55,000 people gained the right to vote. In August 2024 the Minnesota Supreme Court rejected a challenge to the law.

    About 55,000 people regained eligibility; AP reported no count of how many have since registered or voted.

    Minnesota · 2023 to 2024 · Source: Associated Press, Minnesota Supreme Court upholds law restoring right to vote to people with felony convictions, 2024

    How it works
    Lifetime or confusing voting exclusions after a criminal conviction keep people from rejoining political life.
    Evidence
    Documented. The Sentencing Project, an advocacy organization, estimated that about 4.0 million people were barred from voting by a felony conviction in 2024, including 4.5% of Black adults compared with 1.3% of other adults. The estimate comes from a model built on correctional data.
    Response
    States, and Congress where it has authority, would restore voting rights on release from prison, notify eligible people automatically and remove payment conditions that make voting depend on wealth.
    Who acts
    States; Congress where authorized
    Tradeoff
    Eligibility law varies by state, and constitutional litigation may be needed.
    Success looks like
    Registrations by people whose rights were restored, and eligibility errors.
  • DC and territorial residents have no vote in CongressIn the real world: Congress overturned a DC law without a DC voteDocumentedI021

    About 700,000 people in Washington, DC, along with residents of the U.S. territories, have no voting member of the House or Senate. Changing that takes legislation or a constitutional amendment, and territorial residents' own choices about political status.

    The problem, in the real world

    Congress overturned a DC law without a DC vote

    In March 2023, the House voted 250-173 to overturn the District of Columbia's rewrite of its criminal code, and the Senate and President Biden followed. Congress had not nullified a DC law this way in more than three decades. DC's only member of Congress, Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton, holds a nonvoting seat.

    Washington, DC · 2023 · Source: Associated Press, Biden upends politics, precedent in pivot on DC crime law, 2023

    A fix, in the real world

    A 1961 amendment gave DC a vote for president

    The Twenty-third Amendment, ratified on March 29, 1961, gave District of Columbia residents presidential electors, capped at the number held by the least populous state. DC residents first voted for president in 1964. The amendment left them without a voting member of Congress.

    DC has taken part in every presidential election since 1964, while its seat in Congress remains nonvoting.

    Washington, DC · 1961 · Source: National Archives (Reagan Library blog), Constitutional Amendments Series: Amendment XXIII, Extending the Vote to the District of Columbia, 2022

    How it works
    Residents of Washington, DC and the U.S. territories have no voting representation in Congress.
    Evidence
    Documented. The Census Bureau puts the District of Columbia's population at about 700,000, and the District has no voting member of the House or Senate.
    Response
    Congress would pursue representation for DC and a political status for each territory chosen by its residents, through lawful legislation and, where needed, a constitutional amendment.
    Who acts
    Congress; affected residents
    Tradeoff
    Residents' consent, the constitutional structure and territorial self-determination all have to be respected.
    Success looks like
    Residents with full voting representation in Congress.
  • Map-drawers lock in a party's seatsIn the real world: Both parties drew congressional maps to win seatsWell supportedI022

    Officials who draw district lines can arrange them so their party keeps its seats even as voters change their minds. Federal courts do not hear these claims, so state rules and commissions decide how far it goes.

    The problem, in the real world

    Both parties drew congressional maps to win seats

    In North Carolina, Republican legislator David Lewis proposed a 2016 congressional map electing 10 Republicans and 3 Democrats, and Republicans won 10 of 13 seats. Maryland Democrats in 2011 moved about 360,000 voters out of one district to flip it. In Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), the Supreme Court ruled federal courts cannot hear such claims.

    North Carolina and Maryland · 2011 to 2019 · Source: Supreme Court of the United States, Rucho v. Common Cause, 2019

    A fix, in the real world

    Arizona voters handed map-drawing to an independent commission

    Arizona voters adopted Proposition 106 in 2000, moving congressional map-drawing from the legislature to an independent commission. No more than two of its five members may belong to the same party, and the chair must come from outside those parties. The legislature sued, and in 2015 the Supreme Court upheld the commission 5-4.

    The ruling let voter-created commissions keep drawing congressional maps; the Court cited studies finding that commissions draw maps on time and create more competitive districts.

    Arizona · 2000 to 2015 · Source: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (Supreme Court opinion), Arizona State Legislature v. Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission, 2015

    How it works
    When the party in power draws district maps, it can entrench itself despite shifts in voters' preferences.
    Evidence
    Well supported. In Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), the Supreme Court ruled that federal courts cannot hear partisan gerrymandering claims; state law and other federal voting protections still apply. Warshaw, McGhee and Migurski (2022) found that maps drawn by commissions and courts in the 2021 to 2022 cycle showed less partisan bias than maps drawn by legislatures, using descriptive measures from one cycle. The Congressional Research Service has documented the mid-decade redraws of 2025 and 2026.
    Response
    States, and Congress for House elections, would give map-drawing to independent commissions, publish draft maps, set explicit neutral criteria and allow enforceable review in state courts.
    Who acts
    States; Congress for House rules
    Tradeoff
    Geography limits how many districts can be competitive, and neutral criteria can conflict with protecting minority voters' ability to elect candidates.
    Success looks like
    Partisan bias measured across a range of possible vote outcomes, and districts where minority voters can elect their preferred candidates.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-04 Independent citizen commissions draw election maps. Moves map-drawing away from the majority whose seats the map would protect.
    • ReformR-03 Proportional elections in multi-seat House districts. Proportional counting in multi-member districts makes seat shares follow vote shares, so district lines matter less.
  • District lines and at-large elections can dilute minority votesIn the real world: Alabama's map gave Black voters one district of sevenDocumentedI023

    How districts are drawn, or electing a whole council at large, can keep a protected racial group from electing its preferred candidates. After the Supreme Court's 2026 Callais decision, the legal standard for a remedy is much harder to meet.

    The problem, in the real world

    Alabama's map gave Black voters one district of seven

    Alabama's 2021 congressional map had seven districts and only one in which Black voters made up a majority of the voting-age population. A three-judge federal court found the map likely violated the Voting Rights Act. In Allen v. Milligan (2023), the Supreme Court affirmed that finding.

    Alabama · 2021 to 2023 · Source: Supreme Court of the United States, Allen v. Milligan, 2023

    A fix, in the real world

    Louisiana's second Black-majority district was struck down

    After a federal judge found in 2022 that Louisiana's congressional map likely violated the Voting Rights Act, the state enacted a new map, SB8, with a second majority-Black district. In Louisiana v. Callais, decided April 29, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that SB8 was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander.

    The remedy did not hold, and voters bringing such claims must now control for party and present evidence supporting a strong inference of intentional discrimination.

    Louisiana · 2024 to 2026 · Source: Supreme Court of the United States, Louisiana v. Callais, 2026

    How it works
    District lines and at-large election rules can reduce the effective voting strength of groups protected by the Voting Rights Act.
    Evidence
    Documented. In Allen v. Milligan (2023), the Supreme Court found that Alabama's congressional map likely diluted Black votes under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Shelby County v. Holder (2013) struck down the formula that decided which places needed federal approval before changing voting rules, leaving the rest of the Act in place. Louisiana v. Callais (April 29, 2026) revised how courts analyze Section 2 districting claims; it left Section 2 in force and did not bar every majority-minority district.
    Response
    Congress, the Justice Department, the states and the courts would enforce voting-rights protections and adopt district or proportional remedies that have held up in court, with input from affected communities.
    Who acts
    Congress; DOJ; states; courts
    Tradeoff
    Each case and remedy has to be checked against current doctrine. Callais changes Section 2 districting standards substantially, so a current analysis of race and party voting patterns has to come before any remedy is designed.
    Success looks like
    Whether protected groups can elect their preferred candidates, and gaps in access to voting.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-03 Proportional elections in multi-seat House districts. Proportional counting lets a cohesive group win seats in proportion to its votes without depending on single-district lines.
  • Winner-take-all districts can leave large groups of voters with few seatsIn the real world: Single-seat districts turned close votes into lopsided delegationsDocumentedI024

    When the top vote-getter takes a district's only seat, a party with substantial support across a state can win few of that state's seats. Nationally the 2024 House result was close to each party's vote share; the gaps appear inside individual states and in uncontested seats.

    The problem, in the real world

    Single-seat districts turned close votes into lopsided delegations

    In 2016, Republican House candidates in North Carolina won 10 of 13 seats with 53% of the statewide vote. In Maryland, Democrats won 7 of 8 seats in every election from 2012 to 2018 while never topping 65% of the vote. Justice Elena Kagan cited both results in her dissent in Rucho v. Common Cause.

    North Carolina and Maryland · 2012 to 2018 · Source: Supreme Court of the United States, Rucho v. Common Cause (Kagan, J., dissenting), 2019

    How it works
    Single-member districts decided by plurality can turn a party's statewide vote share into a much smaller or larger share of that state's seats. In 2024 the national House result was close to proportional; the distortion appears within states and in seats left uncontested.
    Evidence
    Documented. Federal law (2 U.S.C. 2c) requires single-member House districts, so each state's delegation is chosen one winner-take-all seat at a time. Nationally the 2024 split of House seats came close to the split of votes; the disproportion shows up in individual states and in seats without major-party competition.
    Response
    Congress would authorize multi-member House districts elected by single transferable vote or another tested proportional method. State legislatures would draw them and keep protections for minority voters.
    Who acts
    Congress; state legislatures
    Tradeoff
    Party competition and the way members serve constituents would change, and voters and officials would need education and tested ballots. The post-Callais legal framework has to be checked before adoption.
    Success looks like
    How closely each state's seat shares match its vote shares, and whether voters have meaningful choices.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-03 Proportional elections in multi-seat House districts. Multi-member districts with proportional counting are the direct response to winner-take-all seat distortion.
  • Similar candidates split the vote and push voters off their first choiceIn the real world: Maine elected a governor with 38% of the voteWell supportedI025

    When two similar candidates run, they can divide their supporters and let a third candidate win with less than a majority. Voters who see this coming often abandon their favorite to avoid helping the candidate they like least.

    The problem, in the real world

    Maine elected a governor with 38% of the vote

    In Maine's 2010 race for governor, Republican Paul LePage won with 38% of the vote in a divided field of four candidates. The National Conference of State Legislatures notes the race is often cited when supporters of ranked-choice voting argue that candidates should need at least 50% of the vote to win.

    Maine · 2010 · Source: National Conference of State Legislatures, Ranked Choice Voting, 2026

    A fix, in the real world

    Maine now ranks candidates in primaries and federal races

    Maine first used ranked-choice voting in its June 12, 2018 primary. Voters now rank candidates in all state primaries and in general elections for federal offices, including president. A 2017 advisory opinion from Maine's highest court said the state constitution bars it in general elections for governor and the legislature.

    Ranked ballots now settle Maine's primaries and federal general elections, but a governor's general election like the 2010 race still counts first choices only.

    Maine · 2018 to present · Source: Maine Secretary of State, Bureau of Corporations, Elections and Commissions, Ranked-Choice Voting FAQ, 2026

    How it works
    Under plurality rules, similar candidates split their shared support, and voters abandon their first choice to avoid a worse outcome.
    Evidence
    Well supported. The spoiler effect follows from the counting rule: when only first choices count, supporters of two similar candidates divide their votes. The sources listed for this record study the ranked alternative and give no count of U.S. races decided by a spoiler.
    Response
    States and cities would pilot single-winner ranked-choice voting or another majority method, with clear counting rules, full release of ballot data and audits.
    Who acts
    States; cities
    Tradeoff
    Ranked counting leaves some ballots exhausted and can produce nonmonotonic results, where ranking a candidate higher causes that candidate to lose. It elects one winner per seat, so it leaves proportional representation unchanged.
    Success looks like
    Ballot errors, exhausted ballots, and a published definition of the support a winner needs.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-02 Ranked-choice voting for single-winner races. Ranked ballots transfer to a later choice, which removes the penalty for running or voting for a similar candidate.
    • ReformR-47 Fusion voting and public funding for parties. Fusion voting lets two parties nominate the same candidate, so allied parties can combine support instead of splitting it.
  • Closed primaries shut unaffiliated voters out of the deciding electionIn the real world: Millions of independents locked out of 2024 primariesDocumentedI026

    In a closed primary only voters enrolled in a party can help choose its nominee. Where the primary effectively decides the seat, unaffiliated voters have no say in the contest that settles it.

    The problem, in the real world

    Millions of independents locked out of 2024 primaries

    Unite America, a group that campaigns for open primaries, counted 15.7 million registered independents in 15 states who could not vote in their state's closed primaries in 2024. The group estimated that 87% of U.S. House races were effectively decided in primaries that year.

    15 states with closed primaries · 2024 · Source: Unite America, Analysis: 87% of U.S. House elections already determined in primaries by just 7% of Americans, 2024

    A fix, in the real world

    Alaska opened its primary to every voter

    Alaska voters approved an initiative in the 2020 general election creating a nonpartisan primary in which each voter picks one candidate per race, regardless of party. The four candidates with the most votes advance to a ranked-choice general election. The primary was first used on August 16, 2022.

    Voters of any party, or none, choose from the same primary ballot; the source gives no measure of any change in who takes part.

    Alaska · 2020 to 2026 · Source: Alaska Division of Elections, Ranked Choice Voting (information page), 2026

    How it works
    Party-membership rules restrict who can vote in nomination contests, and in safe seats those contests decide who takes office.
    Evidence
    Documented. Ballotpedia's 2026 state-by-state count classifies each state's primary as closed, semi-closed, open, top-two or top-four. California and Washington use top-two primaries, and Alaska uses a top-four primary with a ranked general election. Massachusetts Question 3, on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would replace party primaries with a single primary in which the top two finishers advance, without ranked ballots.
    Response
    States and parties would compare semi-open primaries, nonpartisan qualifying elections and party-run nominations, judged by who participates and what choices voters get.
    Who acts
    States; parties
    Tradeoff
    Parties have a constitutional right of association that limits how far states can open their nominations, and evidence that open primaries produce more moderate legislators is mixed.
    Success looks like
    Participation among eligible voters, the range of candidates, and how well voters understand the ballot.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-01 All-party primaries with ranked general elections. An all-party primary lets every voter take part in the contest that narrows the field.
  • Ballot-access rules make it harder for new candidates to runIn the real world: Ohio made independents file 229 days before the electionPlausibleI027

    States set signature counts, fees and filing deadlines for getting on the ballot, and these are often heavier for minor parties and independents. High hurdles can keep credible challengers out of a race.

    The problem, in the real world

    Ohio made independents file 229 days before the election

    Ohio required independent presidential candidates in 1980 to file by March 20, 229 days before the election and months before the major parties picked nominees. John Anderson declared his independent run on April 24, 1980, after the deadline had passed. He and his supporters sued over the rule.

    Ohio · 1980 · Source: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (Supreme Court opinion), Anderson v. Celebrezze, 460 U.S. 780, 1983

    A fix, in the real world

    The Supreme Court struck down Ohio's early deadline

    In Anderson v. Celebrezze (1983), the Supreme Court ruled, with four Justices dissenting, that Ohio's March deadline placed an unconstitutional burden on the voting and associational rights of Anderson's supporters. The Court said such a burden discriminates against voters whose political preferences lie outside the existing parties.

    The deadline fell; the Court noted that the major parties would not adopt their nominees for another five months after it.

    Ohio · 1983 · Source: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (Supreme Court opinion), Anderson v. Celebrezze, 460 U.S. 780, 1983

    How it works
    Petition and filing requirements deter credible challengers, and the size of the barrier depends on each state's rules.
    Evidence
    Plausible. Ballotpedia's 2026 state-by-state tables document signature and fee requirements that are heavier for minor-party and independent candidates than for major-party nominees. The tables show the rules; no study listed for this record measures how many credible candidates they deter.
    Response
    States would set signature thresholds in proportion to the size of the electorate and uniform filing deadlines. Debate sponsors would adopt neutral criteria for who gets on stage.
    Who acts
    States; debate sponsors
    Tradeoff
    Thresholds set too low lengthen ballots and add work for election offices.
    Success looks like
    Candidates who qualify, signatures rejected, and how many viewers debates reach.
  • Equal Senate seats give small-state residents more weightDocumentedI028

    Every state has two senators whatever its population, so a resident of a small state has far more Senate representation per person than a resident of a large one. Article V of the Constitution bars changing a state's equal Senate vote without that state's consent.

    How it works
    Equal Senate seats for every state give residents of small states far more national influence per person.
    Evidence
    Documented. The 2020 Census counted California at about 39.5 million residents and Wyoming at about 577,000, roughly 68 to 1, and each state elects two senators.
    Response
    Congress and the states would analyze options for admitting states and for representation, and would pursue any constitutional change toward population equality with Article V's limits stated openly.
    Who acts
    Congress; states
    Tradeoff
    Article V protects each state's equal Senate vote unless that state consents to a change.
    Success looks like
    Residents per senator across states, and the size of the representation gap.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-50 Popular-vote compact and constitutional amendment options. Keeps Senate apportionment options under examination with Article V's constraints explicit.
  • The Electoral College can elect the national vote's runner-upIn the real world: Bush won in 2000 with fewer popular votes than GoreDocumentedI029

    Because most states give all their electoral votes to the statewide winner, a candidate can win the presidency with fewer votes nationwide. The alternatives, a constitutional amendment or an interstate compact, each carry legal questions.

    The problem, in the real world

    Bush won in 2000 with fewer popular votes than Gore

    In 2000, George W. Bush won the presidency with 271 electoral votes to Al Gore's 266, though Gore received more popular votes nationwide, the National Archives notes. Bush carried all 25 of Florida's electoral votes, which put him past the 270 needed.

    United States (decided by Florida) · 2000 · Source: National Archives, 2000 Electoral College Results, 2000

    A fix, in the real world

    Eighteen states and DC signed a popular-vote compact

    Eighteen states and the District of Columbia have enacted the National Popular Vote compact, which would award their electoral votes to the national vote winner. By the count of National Popular Vote, the group promoting it, members hold 222 electoral votes. It takes effect only once members reach 270.

    The compact has not taken effect; it needs states holding 48 more electoral votes.

    18 states and the District of Columbia · 2026 · Source: National Popular Vote, State status of the National Popular Vote bill, 2026

    How it works
    Allocating electoral votes state by state can elect a president who lost the national popular vote.
    Evidence
    Documented. In the 2000 and 2016 presidential elections, the Electoral College winner received fewer popular votes nationwide than the runner-up.
    Response
    Congress and the states would compare direct popular election by constitutional amendment with the interstate compact, planning for litigation and for how each would operate.
    Who acts
    Congress; states
    Tradeoff
    The compact's validity and operation remain contested, and no simple federal statute can replace the Electoral College nationwide.
    Success looks like
    Whether the presidential winner matches the national popular-vote winner, and how widely campaigns spread their attention across states.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-50 Popular-vote compact and constitutional amendment options. Covers both an Electoral College amendment and the National Popular Vote compact.
  • Threats and pressure drive election officials outIn the real world: Nearly 4 in 10 local election officials report threatsWell supportedI030

    Local election officials face threats and pressure over counting and certifying results, duties the law defines. Experienced staff leave, and the personal cost of serving rises.

    The problem, in the real world

    Nearly 4 in 10 local election officials report threats

    In a Brennan Center survey of 858 local election officials taken in April and May 2025, 38% said they had faced threats, harassment or abuse because of their job. More than half, 52%, said they were concerned about the safety of their colleagues and staff.

    United States (local election offices) · 2025 · Source: Brennan Center for Justice, Local Election Officials Survey, July 2025 (report PDF), 2025

    How it works
    Partisan pressure over counting and certification, along with threats, politicizes legal duties and drives experienced staff out of election work.
    Evidence
    Well supported. In the Brennan Center's survey of 858 local election officials (April to May 2025), 38% reported threats, harassment or abuse, 52% worried about their staff's safety and 60% worried about federal cuts to election security support.
    Response
    States, Congress and the Justice Department would professionalize election administration, protect certification as a defined legal duty and fund threat response under public standards.
    Who acts
    States; Congress; DOJ
    Tradeoff
    Independent election offices still need accountable appointments and public audits.
    Success looks like
    Vacancies in election offices, threats reported, and certifications completed on time and as the law requires.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-45 Verifiable elections with paper records and audits. Protects election officials and makes certification a scheduled legal duty.
  • Election offices run on irregular fundingIn the real world: Federal election security grants rise and fall each yearPlausibleI031

    U.S. elections cost about $2 billion a year, paid mostly by local governments on an irregular basis. Old equipment and staff turnover raise the risk of errors and security problems.

    The problem, in the real world

    Federal election security grants rise and fall each year

    Congress has funded federal election security grants to states only in some years since 2018, with no new money in 2019 or 2021. It appropriated $15 million for fiscal 2025 and $45 million for fiscal 2026, and states must add a 20% match.

    United States · 2018 to 2026 · Source: U.S. Election Assistance Commission, Election Security Funds, 2026

    How it works
    Aging equipment and staff turnover increase errors and security weaknesses in election administration.
    Evidence
    Plausible. The MIT Election Data and Science Lab's 2021 synthesis estimated that elections cost roughly $2 billion a year nationally, with funding that is local and irregular. In the Brennan Center's 2025 survey of 858 local election officials, 60% worried about federal cuts to security support. Neither source measures error rates.
    Response
    Congress and the states would provide recurring formula grants for paper records, risk-limiting audits, cybersecurity and trained staff.
    Who acts
    Congress; states
    Tradeoff
    Federal requirements should come with funding, and equipment contracts should avoid locking offices into one vendor.
    Success looks like
    Audits completed, age of voting equipment, and recovery exercises held.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-45 Verifiable elections with paper records and audits. Sets the floor of paper records and audits that recurring grants would pay for.
  • Late rule changes and slow rulings shake confidence in resultsIn the real world: Wisconsin's ballot deadline changed in the final days before votingPlausibleI032

    When voting rules change close to an election, voters and poll workers struggle to keep up. If disputes then take too long to settle, access suffers and fewer people accept the result.

    The problem, in the real world

    Wisconsin's ballot deadline changed in the final days before voting

    Five days before Wisconsin's April 7, 2020 election, a federal judge extended the absentee deadline and let ballots mailed after Election Day count. On April 6 the Supreme Court blocked that part, saying lower courts should not alter election rules on the eve of an election. Four dissenters warned that tens of thousands of voters might not get their requested ballots in time.

    Wisconsin · 2020 · Source: Supreme Court of the United States, Republican National Committee v. Democratic National Committee (per curiam), 2020

    A fix, in the real world

    Congress rewrote the electoral vote count rules in 2022

    The Electoral Count Reform Act, enacted in December 2022, limits the vice president's role in counting electoral votes to solely ministerial duties. An objection to a state's electoral votes now needs the signatures of one-fifth of both the Senate and the House, and only two grounds are allowed.

    Its first use came with the count of the 2024 electoral votes in January 2025, which proceeded as the law describes.

    United States Congress · 2022 to 2025 · Source: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School, 3 U.S. Code 15, Counting electoral votes in Congress (as amended by Pub. L. 117-328), 2022

    How it works
    Rule changes late in an election cycle and slow resolution of disputes reduce access to voting and acceptance of results.
    Evidence
    Plausible. In Watson v. Republican National Committee (2026), the Supreme Court ruled that federal Election Day statutes do not bar counting mail ballots postmarked by Election Day, one example of rules litigated close to an election. No source listed for this record measures the effect of late changes on turnout or acceptance.
    Response
    States, and Congress within its authority, would publish rules early and set up fast, neutral adjudication with clear certification deadlines and defined remedies.
    Who acts
    States; Congress within authority
    Tradeoff
    Emergencies still require limited exceptions, subject to court review.
    Success looks like
    Rule changes made late in the cycle, contests unresolved at deadlines, and compliance with certification dates.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-45 Verifiable elections with paper records and audits. Requires certification on a schedule, which narrows the window for late disputes.
  • State takeovers move local decisions away from local votersIn the real world: Flint's state-appointed managers switched the city's waterPlausibleI166

    States can override local governments or replace local boards, including county election boards. Power then shifts to officials whom local residents cannot vote out.

    The problem, in the real world

    Flint's state-appointed managers switched the city's water

    In 2014, state-appointed emergency managers running Flint, Michigan, switched the city's water source to the Flint River. A task force appointed by Governor Rick Snyder found in 2016 that the managers made that decision in place of locally elected officials. It said the structure made it extremely difficult for Flint residents to check decisions.

    Flint, Michigan · 2014 to 2016 · Source: Flint Water Advisory Task Force (State of Michigan), Flint Water Advisory Task Force Final Report, 2016

    How it works
    State preemption and restructuring of local boards move authority away from bodies that local voters elect.
    Evidence
    Plausible. Georgia's 2021 election law (SB 202) authorizes the State Election Board to take over county election administration; how often that power is used is the open empirical question. Grumbach's Laboratories Against Democracy (2022) documents declines in democratic performance at the state level and does not measure the effects of takeovers specifically.
    Response
    State legislatures and state courts would require published criteria for any takeover, due process, a time limit and independent review, and would protect lawful local autonomy in state law. Residents would be able to invoke these protections.
    Who acts
    State legislatures; state courts; residents
    Tradeoff
    States hold broad constitutional authority over local governments, and its limits differ by state.
    Success looks like
    Stated reasons for takeovers, outcomes of review, and voting access in affected places.
  • A fixed-size House makes districts larger as the population growsIn the real world: House districts have more than tripled in size since 1911PlausibleI174

    The House has stayed at 435 seats for more than a century while the population grew, so each member now represents about 761,000 people. Larger districts go with less contact between residents and their representative.

    The problem, in the real world

    House districts have more than tripled in size since 1911

    Congress capped the House at 435 seats in the Apportionment Act of 1911, when the average member represented roughly 212,000 people. After the 2010 Census the average was about 710,000, and the Census Bureau put it at 761,169 after 2020.

    United States · 1911 to 2020 · Source: U.S. House of Representatives, History, Art and Archives, Proportional Representation, 2026

    How it works
    Keeping the House at a fixed size while the population grows raises the number of constituents each member serves.
    Evidence
    Plausible. After the 2020 Census the average House district held 761,169 residents. Frederick (2010) found that larger districts go with less constituent contact and lower approval of the member; the evidence is observational and the effects modest.
    Response
    Congress would evaluate expanding the House with a published apportionment rule, a plan for staff and facilities, and coordination with any change to how districts elect members.
    Who acts
    Congress
    Tradeoff
    More seats alone would leave disproportionality, gerrymandering and responsiveness unchanged.
    Success looks like
    Residents per member, constituents' access to their member's office, and the cost of the transition.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-46 Expand the House of Representatives. Adds seats so each member represents fewer people.
  • In safe seats, a small primary electorate picks the winnerIn the real world: Primaries with 7% of eligible voters settled most House seatsWell supportedX01

    In most House districts one party is sure to win in November, so its primary decides who takes office. Turnout in those primaries is a small fraction of eligible voters.

    The problem, in the real world

    Primaries with 7% of eligible voters settled most House seats

    Unite America, a group that advocates primary reform, calculated that 380 U.S. House seats, about 87%, were effectively decided in 2024 primaries. It found those primaries drew 18.1 million voters, about 7% of those eligible, and that 169 members ran unopposed in their primary for a safe seat.

    United States · 2024 · Source: Unite America, Analysis: 87% of U.S. House elections already determined in primaries by just 7% of Americans, 2024

    A fix, in the real world

    Alaska sends four finishers of any party to November

    Since 2022, Alaska has used one primary open to every voter in place of party primaries, and the top four finishers in each race advance to a ranked-choice general election. Voters approved the change in 2020. Alaskans decide on November 3, 2026 whether to repeal it.

    The record is short, effects on legislators' moderation are contested, and the system faces a repeal vote on November 3, 2026.

    Alaska · 2020 to 2026 · Source: Alaska Division of Elections, Ranked Choice Voting (information page), 2026

    How it works
    Most House seats are effectively decided in low-turnout primaries, which leaves the general election little chance of changing the outcome. Unite America, an advocacy group, puts the 2024 share at about 87% of seats decided by roughly 7% of eligible voters; the exact figures depend on how a safe seat is defined.
    Evidence
    Well supported in direction. Unite America, which advocates primary reform, calculated that about 87% of U.S. House seats were effectively decided in 2024 primaries in which roughly 7% of eligible voters took part; the numbers depend on its threshold for a safe seat. Ballotpedia's 2024 competitiveness report separately counted 38 House races without major-party competition and found that 52% of incumbents faced no contested primary.
    Response
    States, and voters by initiative where allowed, would adopt top-four or all-party primaries with ranked general elections, citizen redistricting commissions or multi-member districts. Massachusetts Question 3, on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would replace party primaries with a single primary in which the top two finishers advance.
    Who acts
    Tradeoff
    Parties lose control of nominations, and some voters lose a ballot line they value. Ranked counts take longer, and a primary that advances two candidates of one party leaves some voters without their party in November.
    Success looks like
    Share of seats with a competitive general election, turnout in the round that decides the seat, and share of incumbents facing a credible challenger in November.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-01 All-party primaries with ranked general elections. Moves the deciding contest to a general election that all voters take part in.
    • ReformR-04 Independent citizen commissions draw election maps. Commission-drawn maps reduce the number of seats made safe by design.
    • ReformR-03 Proportional elections in multi-seat House districts. Multi-member proportional districts make most seats contestable even where geography sorts voters.
  • States ban local voting methods and raise the bar for initiativesIn the real world: Ohio banned ranked ballots in every election, including citiesDocumentedX02

    Nineteen states now bar ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, including city elections. Some legislatures have also tried to make citizen initiatives harder to pass after voters used them.

    The problem, in the real world

    Ohio banned ranked ballots in every election, including cities

    Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed a bill on March 17, 2026, barring any election in the state from using ranked-choice voting. Cities that adopt it lose state local-government fund payments. Ohio became the 19th state with such a ban, weeks after Indiana enacted one in February.

    Ohio · 2026 · Source: Ballotpedia News, Ohio becomes second state this year to ban ranked-choice voting, 2026

    A fix, in the real world

    Ohio voters kept the majority rule for amendments

    Ohio's legislature put a measure on an August 2023 special ballot that would have raised the vote needed to approve constitutional amendments from a simple majority to 60%. Voters rejected it, 57% to 43%, keeping the existing rule.

    Constitutional amendments in Ohio, including those proposed by citizen initiative, still pass with a simple majority of voters.

    Ohio · 2023 · Source: Ballotpedia, Ohio Issue 1, 60% Vote Requirement to Approve Constitutional Amendments Measure (August 2023), 2023

    How it works
    States are banning local use of ranked-choice voting and trying to raise initiative thresholds after voters use them, closing routes residents have used to change election rules.
    Evidence
    Documented. As of March 2026, 19 states prohibit ranked-choice voting by statute; Ohio's ban, signed March 17, 2026, followed Indiana's in February. Ballotpedia reports that 17 of the 19 bans were enacted where Republicans held the governorship and both legislative chambers. In August 2023, Ohio voters rejected, 57% to 43%, a legislature-referred amendment that would have raised the vote needed to approve constitutional amendments to 60%.
    Response
    State legislatures, or voters by initiative, would protect cities' authority to choose their own election method and shield the initiative process from rule changes in the middle of a cycle.
    Who acts
    Tradeoff
    When cities choose their own methods, neighboring places can use different rules, which adds work for county election offices and for voters who move between them.
    Success looks like
    States that ban local election methods, and initiative rules changed in the middle of a cycle.
  • Off-cycle local elections draw fewer and different votersIn the real world: Stand-alone city elections draw about half the votersWell supportedX03

    Cities and school districts that vote in odd years or in spring draw a fraction of November turnout. The smaller electorate is older and more organized, and local decisions answer more to it.

    The problem, in the real world

    Stand-alone city elections draw about half the voters

    Research reviewed by political scientists Zoltan Hajnal, Vladimir Kogan and G. Agustin Markarian finds that local elections held on the November ballot generally draw double the turnout of stand-alone local contests. In California cities, they found the off-cycle electorate was less representative of residents, especially by race and age.

    California cities · 2022 study · Source: Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian, American Political Science Review, Who Votes: City Election Timing and Voter Composition, 2022

    A fix, in the real world

    California cities moved votes to November and widened the electorate

    California cities that moved their elections onto the statewide November ballot drew a broader set of voters. Using voter files, Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian found the on-cycle electorate was considerably more representative of residents, especially when local races coincided with a presidential election.

    Moving on-cycle produced a considerably more representative electorate, and the authors conclude that on-cycle elections can improve local democracy.

    California · 2022 study · Source: Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian, American Political Science Review, Who Votes: City Election Timing and Voter Composition, 2022

    How it works
    Holding local elections in odd years or in spring cuts turnout and gives organized interests a larger say over local government.
    Evidence
    Well supported. Using California voter files, Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian (2022) found that moving city elections to the November ballot roughly doubles turnout and makes the electorate more representative of residents. Kogan, Lavertu and Peskowitz (2018) found that off-cycle school-district elections shifted the electorate and went with higher teacher pay than in on-cycle districts. Anzia's Timing and Turnout (2014) documents the turnout gap and the larger role of organized groups in off-cycle contests.
    Response
    States by mandate, and cities through their charters, would move local elections onto the November ballot.
    Who acts
    Tradeoff
    Ballots get longer, and some voters skip local races listed below national ones.
    Success looks like
    Local turnout, the mix of ages and of renters and owners among local voters, and housing approvals.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-06 Hold local elections alongside November races. Moves local elections to the November ballot, which is this record's response.
  • Party organizations still steer who gets nominatedIn the real world: Alaska's lieutenant governor quit a House race after the primaryWell supportedX11

    Party committees shape who runs and who survives a primary through endorsements, money and pressure on candidates to step aside. A June 2026 Supreme Court ruling lets parties coordinate unlimited spending with their candidates.

    The problem, in the real world

    Alaska's lieutenant governor quit a House race after the primary

    Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, a Republican, finished third with about 20% in Alaska's 2024 top-four primary for the U.S. House, enough to advance, then withdrew. Many local Republican groups had endorsed Nick Begich, and a political consultant said two Republicans running against one Democrat would be a tough path.

    Alaska · 2024 · Source: Alaska Beacon, Lt. Gov. Dahlstrom quits U.S. House race after finishing behind Peltola and Begich in the primary, 2024

    How it works
    Party organizations shape who can win a nomination by steering endorsements, money and candidate entry. The 2026 ruling ending limits on coordinated party spending, and the spread of state bans on ranked-choice voting, add to that influence relative to primary reforms driven by voters.
    Evidence
    Well supported. On June 30, 2026, in NRSC v. FEC, the Supreme Court ruled that federal limits on spending parties coordinate with their candidates violate the First Amendment, overruling its earlier precedent. In Alaska's 2024 top-four primary, Lieutenant Governor Nancy Dahlstrom finished third with about 20% and withdrew, with Republican consultants citing the risk of two Republicans splitting the vote against one Democrat; it is a single case. The Party Decides (Cohen and colleagues, 2008) argues that party insiders effectively pick presidential nominees through endorsements before voters engage, a thesis contested since 2016 and limited to presidential races. Nineteen states ban ranked-choice voting by statute as of March 2026.
    Response
    States and Congress would consider fusion voting and public funding directed to parties, require parties to publish their dues schedules, and treat party rules as part of the rules that govern elections.
    Who acts
    Tradeoff
    Fusion voting and party-centered funding can strengthen party leaders.
    Success looks like
    Minor-party ballot lines that win votes, and how long coalitions last.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-47 Fusion voting and public funding for parties. Fusion voting and party-centered funding give organized coalitions a route that party committees do not control alone.

Taking part, trust and shared norms 6

  • Hostility toward the other party leads voters to excuse their own sideIn the real world: Fewer hardline Montana voters punished an attack on a reporterWell supportedI149

    When partisans dislike or fear the other party, many will still vote for their own candidate after that candidate breaks democratic rules. That weakens the electoral cost of misconduct, though researchers dispute how much.

    The problem, in the real world

    Fewer hardline Montana voters punished an attack on a reporter

    In 2017, Republican candidate Greg Gianforte body-slammed a reporter in his campaign office the night before Montana's congressional election, when more than half of voters had already cast absentee ballots. Yale researchers found that Election Day voters in politically moderate precincts punished him by voting across party lines, while significantly fewer did so in hardline Republican precincts.

    Montana · 2017 · Source: Government Executive (republished from Yale News), Most U.S. Voters Value Party Over Democracy, 2020

    A fix, in the real world

    Washington's climate assembly brought rival viewpoints to shared work

    In early 2021, 80 Washington residents chosen by lottery spent seven weeks online writing climate recommendations for the Legislature. Evaluators from the Clinton School of Public Service reported a decrease in sensitivity to polarization and a willingness to work together among people with different viewpoints and political identities.

    The findings were preliminary and covered only assembly members, so lasting or wider effects are unmeasured.

    Washington State · 2021 · Source: Clinton School of Public Service, University of Arkansas, Park, Richards, Noori Present Evaluation Findings to Washington State Climate Assembly, 2021

    How it works
    Hostility toward the other party leads partisans to excuse misconduct by their own side.
    Evidence
    Well supported. In Graham and Svolik's 2020 experiments, only about 3.5% of voters were willing to defect from their party's candidate over an undemocratic position in realistic matchups, although the average penalty in vote share was 11.7 points. Iyengar and colleagues (2019) review the causes and consequences of affective polarization, the dislike of the other party's supporters. Broockman, Kalla and Westwood (2023) found that affective polarization does not clearly reduce accountability, so the link is contested.
    Response
    Civic groups, parties and local institutions would organize structured cross-party work on concrete shared problems and apply equal standards to political conduct.
    Who acts
    Civic groups; parties; local institutions
    Tradeoff
    Contact reduces hostility only under certain conditions, and surface civility cannot settle conflicts over rights.
    Success looks like
    Attitudes toward the other party, joint work across parties, and consistent application of conduct standards.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-49 Civic work that crosses party lines. Cross-partisan membership and service is the structured contact this record proposes.
  • Scapegoating divides people who could work togetherIn the real world: Boston commuters grew less welcoming after brief contactPlausibleI150

    Blaming racial or identity groups for hardship can pull attention away from the institutions that cause it. It also denies people equal standing and splits potential coalitions.

    The problem, in the real world

    Boston commuters grew less welcoming after brief contact

    In July and August 2012, Harvard researcher Ryan Enos placed Spanish speakers working for his study on commuter rail platforms in largely Anglo-white Boston-area towns for 10 working days. Regular riders who saw them shifted toward wanting fewer immigrants from Mexico and opposing letting undocumented immigrants stay, though the effect may have weakened with repeated contact.

    Boston area, Massachusetts · 2012 · Source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Causal effect of intergroup contact on exclusionary attitudes (Enos), PNAS 111(10), author copy, 2014

    A fix, in the real world

    Door-to-door conversations eased hostility toward immigrants for months

    In field experiments published in 2020, political scientists Joshua Kalla and David Broockman tested door-to-door conversations in which canvassers and voters swapped personal stories without judgment. Across three experiments, 230 canvassers talked with 6,869 voters in seven U.S. locations, and the first experiment reduced exclusionary attitudes toward unauthorized immigrants for at least four months.

    The effect was small, about 0.08 of a standard deviation, and two later experiments on attitudes toward transgender people found similar results.

    Seven U.S. locations · 2020 · Source: American Political Science Review 114(2), Reducing Exclusionary Attitudes through Interpersonal Conversation: Evidence from Three Field Experiments (Kalla, Broockman), 2020

    How it works
    Scapegoating diverts grievances from institutional causes and denies equal standing.
    Evidence
    Plausible. Sides, Tesler and Vavreck's Identity Crisis (2018) found from surveys that identity attitudes predicted vote shifts in 2016 more than economic distress did. In a field experiment, Enos (2014) found that brief exposure to members of an outgroup increased exclusionary attitudes.
    Response
    Schools, civic groups and parties would protect equal participation and create local forums that connect material problems to evidence without blaming whole groups.
    Who acts
    Schools; civic groups; parties
    Tradeoff
    Dialogue requires safety and equal status for those taking part.
    Success looks like
    Gaps in participation, and discriminatory incidents.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-49 Civic work that crosses party lines. Repeated shared work across groups is the kind of contact this record's response relies on.
  • Parties tolerate conduct that weakens democratic rulesIn the real world: Each party mostly shielded its own member from censureWell supportedI153

    When voters rarely punish their own side, parties pay little price for nominating or protecting members who deny election results or intimidate opponents. Party rules and discipline are one place this can be checked.

    The problem, in the real world

    Each party mostly shielded its own member from censure

    In November 2021, the House censured Republican Paul Gosar for posting a cartoon that depicted violence against Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez; 207 Republicans voted no and 2 voted yes. In December 2023, it censured Democrat Jamaal Bowman, who had pleaded guilty to falsely pulling a fire alarm; 191 Democrats voted no and 3 voted yes.

    U.S. House of Representatives · 2021 and 2023 · Source: Office of the Clerk, U.S. House of Representatives, Roll Call 379: H.Res. 789, Censuring Representative Paul Gosar, 2021

    How it works
    Electoral incentives reward parties that tolerate election denial, intimidation or abuse by their members.
    Evidence
    Well supported. Graham and Svolik (2020) found that only about 3.5% of voters would defect from their party's candidate over an undemocratic position in realistic matchups. Levitsky and Ziblatt's How Democracies Die (2018) argues from comparative history that party gatekeeping is a central safeguard. Bright Line Watch surveys of experts and the public track the erosion of democratic norms through 2026.
    Response
    Political parties and civic organizations would adopt enforceable standards for nominations and conduct, with transparent disciplinary procedures.
    Who acts
    Political parties; civic organizations
    Tradeoff
    Gatekeeping needs internal democracy and due process.
    Success looks like
    Compliance with party rules, and consistent sanctions.
  • Threats and violence raise the cost of public lifeIn the real world: Threats against Congress jumped to nearly 15,000 casesDocumentedI154

    The U.S. Capitol Police opened 14,938 threat cases in 2025, the third straight annual rise, and 43% of state legislators surveyed reported threats. When serving in office or speaking up invites danger, fewer people take part.

    The problem, in the real world

    Threats against Congress jumped to nearly 15,000 cases

    In 2025, the U.S. Capitol Police's threat assessment unit investigated 14,938 concerning statements aimed at members of Congress, up from 9,474 in 2024. It was the third straight yearly increase and the highest count in the five years the agency reported.

    United States · 2025 · Source: U.S. Capitol Police, USCP Threat Assessment Cases for 2025, 2026

    A fix, in the real world

    Capitol Police tripled local protection agreements in 2025

    In 2025, the U.S. Capitol Police tripled its formal agreements with local law enforcement agencies that help protect members of Congress in their home districts. It has also detailed its own attorneys to the Justice Department, where they have consulted with agents on 875 cases and worked on 1,705 subpoenas.

    Threat cases still rose sharply that year, and no evaluation has measured whether these steps prevented violence.

    United States · 2025 · Source: U.S. Capitol Police, USCP Threat Assessment Cases for 2025, 2026

    How it works
    Threats raise the personal cost of public service and of public disagreement.
    Evidence
    Documented. The U.S. Capitol Police opened 14,938 threat-assessment cases in 2025, the third straight annual increase. In a 2024 Brennan Center survey, 43% of state legislators reported threats.
    Response
    The Justice Department, the states and local law enforcement would fund lawful threat prevention, protect people who are targeted and prosecute violence under viewpoint-neutral standards.
    Who acts
    DOJ; states; local law enforcement
    Tradeoff
    Broad labels of extremism can chill lawful protest.
    Success looks like
    Threat cases resolved, safety of victims, and public participation.
  • Unsupported fraud claims weaken acceptance of defeatIn the real world: Appeals court refused to block Pennsylvania's 2020 certified resultDocumentedI155

    After the 2020 election, claims of fraud large enough to change the outcome failed in court, and a review by conservative lawyers found no supporting evidence in any of 64 cases. Such claims still threaten the peaceful transfer of power when officials act on them.

    The problem, in the real world

    Appeals court refused to block Pennsylvania's 2020 certified result

    In November 2020, the Trump campaign asked a federal appeals court to stop Pennsylvania's certified presidential totals, a margin of 80,555 votes, from taking effect. The Third Circuit refused, noting the campaign "never alleges that any ballot was fraudulent," and Judge Stephanos Bibas wrote that "calling an election unfair does not make it so."

    Pennsylvania · 2020 · Source: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, Donald J. Trump for President, Inc. v. Secretary, Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, No. 20-3371, 2020

    A fix, in the real world

    Congress raised the bar for objecting to electoral votes

    In December 2022, Congress amended the federal law for counting presidential electoral votes. An objection to a state's votes now needs the signatures of at least one-fifth of each chamber's members, and the vice president's role in the count is limited to "solely ministerial duties."

    Congress counted the 2024 electoral votes under these rules on January 6, 2025; whether they raise public acceptance of results is unmeasured.

    United States · 2022 · Source: National Archives, Office of the Federal Register, Provisions of the Constitution and United States Code (Electoral College), n.d.

    How it works
    Unsupported claims of election fraud weaken the peaceful transfer of power.
    Evidence
    Documented. The House Select Committee to Investigate the January 6th Attack on the United States Capitol issued its final report in 2022 on the effort to overturn the 2020 result. Lost, Not Stolen (2022), an independent review by conservative lawyers and former officials, found no evidence of outcome-changing fraud in any of 64 court cases.
    Response
    Election offices, parties and courts would publish audit evidence people can understand, require officials to follow lawful certification and treat concession after a resolved contest as the norm.
    Who acts
    Election offices; parties; courts
    Tradeoff
    Legitimate challenges to results must remain available.
    Success looks like
    Public understanding of audit evidence, and lawful transfers of power.
  • Partisan identity weakens punishment of one's own sideIn the real world: Only 3.5% would vote against their side to punish undemocratic conductWell supportedX09

    For many Americans, party has become a social identity tied to dislike of the other side. In experiments, voters penalized an undemocratic candidate from their own party, yet only about 3.5% were willing to switch their vote over it.

    The problem, in the real world

    Only 3.5% would vote against their side to punish undemocratic conduct

    In 2020, Yale political scientist Milan Svolik and coauthor Matthew Graham reported a nationally representative survey experiment in which Americans chose between hypothetical state legislative candidates. When candidates held their party's usual positions, only 3.5% of respondents would vote against their partisan interests to punish undemocratic conduct. Svolik said voters, regardless of party affiliation, are willing to forgive such behavior.

    United States · 2020 · Source: Government Executive (republished from Yale News), Most U.S. Voters Value Party Over Democracy, 2020

    How it works
    Party has become a social identity, and partisans punish norm-breaking by their own side only weakly: few are willing to switch their vote over it.
    Evidence
    Well supported. In Graham and Svolik's 2020 experiments, a candidate's undemocratic position cost an average of 11.7 points in vote share, while only about 3.5% of respondents were willing to defect from their own party's candidate over it in realistic matchups. Abramowitz and Webster (2016) document the rise since the 1990s of negative partisanship, voting against the other party more than for one's own. Mason's Uncivil Agreement (2018) gives an identity-based account of polarization.
    Response
    States, civic organizations and researchers would adopt electoral rules that reward building coalitions, support institutions that bring people of different parties together and use common-identity messages tested in the 2023 megastudy.
    Who acts
    Tradeoff
    Effects of cross-party contact and messaging fade quickly, within about two weeks in the megastudy.
    Success looks like
    Cross-party membership, and measured animosity among members.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-49 Civic work that crosses party lines. Cross-partisan membership and civic service are the institutions this record proposes.
    • ReformR-02 Ranked-choice voting for single-winner races. Ranked ballots reward candidates who seek second choices from other camps.
    • ReformR-47 Fusion voting and public funding for parties. Fusion voting lets parties form coalitions behind one candidate.

Checks on power and equal justice 5

  • Unpredictable Supreme Court vacancies raise the stakes of each appointmentIn the real world: One president got no picks, another got threeWell supportedI072

    Justices serve for life, so the timing of deaths and retirements decides how many appointments each president gets. Recent confirmations have passed by near party-line votes.

    The problem, in the real world

    One president got no picks, another got three

    The Senate's list of Supreme Court nominations since 1789 shows none from President Jimmy Carter. Donald Trump's three nominees were confirmed in 2017, 2018 and 2020 by margins of two to nine votes. Barack Obama's 2016 nominee, Merrick Garland, received no Senate action and no vote.

    United States (federal) · 1977-2020 · Source: U.S. Senate, Supreme Court Nominations (1789-present), 2026

    A fix, in the real world

    Germany's top court judges serve one 12-year term

    Germany's Federal Constitutional Court has 16 justices, and each one leaves after a single 12-year term or at age 68, with no second term allowed. Half are elected by the Bundestag and half by the Bundesrat, and every pick needs a two-thirds majority in the electing body.

    Terms end on a fixed schedule and each pick needs a two-thirds vote; the source does not measure any effect on how contested appointments are.

    Germany · Current rules · Source: Federal Constitutional Court of Germany (Bundesverfassungsgericht), Organisation (The Federal Constitutional Court), 2026

    How it works
    Lifetime appointments make vacancies unpredictable, so each one becomes a high-stakes contest.
    Evidence
    Well supported. U.S. Senate records show recent Supreme Court confirmations passing by margins of 52 to 48, 50 to 48 and 53 to 47, close to party lines. The 2021 Presidential Commission on the Supreme Court reviewed proposals for term limits and for adding seats.
    Response
    Congress and the states would compare regular 18-year Supreme Court terms, with transition rules, against amendment options, and publish standards for selecting nominees.
    Who acts
    Congress; states
    Tradeoff
    Term limits set by statute are constitutionally disputed, and adding seats to the Court can set off escalation.
    Success looks like
    Predictable appointments, and the Court's legitimacy and independence.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-16 Supreme Court 18-year terms and enforceable ethics. Regular 18-year terms give each presidential term two appointments, removing the role of chance vacancies.
  • Supreme Court ethics complaints have no independent reviewIn the real world: A justice took undisclosed luxury trips for two decadesDocumentedI073

    The Supreme Court adopted a code of conduct in 2023, and no outside body enforces it for the justices. When a court polices itself, complaints and conflicts can go unresolved.

    The problem, in the real world

    A justice took undisclosed luxury trips for two decades
