    In April 2023, ProPublica reported that Justice Clarence Thomas had accepted luxury trips from Dallas businessman Harlan Crow virtually every year for more than two decades without reporting them on his annual financial disclosures. Experts told ProPublica the law required disclosure of private jet flights. The article said the Supreme Court is left almost entirely to police itself, and Thomas publicly defended the trips.

    U.S. Supreme Court · 2023-2025 · Source: ProPublica, Clarence Thomas and the Billionaire, 2023

    A fix, in the real world

    Lower federal judges face a formal complaint process

    The federal courts' Table S-22 counts misconduct complaints against judges under 28 U.S.C. 351-364. In the year ending September 30, 2025, people filed 1,857 complaints. Chief circuit judges dismissed 1,700 in whole or in part, and three complaints were referred to special committees.

    In the same year, four complaints ended with voluntary corrective action, and none led to censure, reprimand, suspension of assignments or any other remedial action.

    U.S. federal courts below the Supreme Court · 1980-2025 · Source: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts, Table S-22: Complaints Filed and Action Taken Under 28 U.S.C. 351-364 (12 months ending September 30, 2025), 2025

    How it works
    Self-policing leaves judicial conflicts and complaints unresolved.
    Evidence
    Documented. The Supreme Court adopted a Code of Conduct on November 13, 2023; it creates no independent process to decide complaints or enforce the code. Fix the Court, an advocacy group, reported in 2025 that the code remains unenforced, that the Judicial Conference dropped a referral concerning Justice Thomas, and that the Supreme Court Ethics, Recusal and Transparency Act had not been enacted.
    Response
    The Supreme Court, or Congress, would publish reasons for recusals, review disclosures and create an independent complaint process consistent with judicial independence.
    Who acts
    Supreme Court; Congress
    Tradeoff
    A 2023 code already exists, and enforcement procedures have to avoid giving either party control over cases.
    Success looks like
    Completeness of disclosures, and how complaints are resolved.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-16 Supreme Court 18-year terms and enforceable ethics. Adds an enforceable ethics process for the justices.
  • At-will removal of regulators narrows agency independenceIn the real world: Two presidents removed FTC commissioners over policyDocumentedI163

    In June 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that the President can remove FTC commissioners at will, and the same day left protection for Federal Reserve governors in place. Whether the change has altered enforcement priorities has not yet been measured.

    The problem, in the real world

    Two presidents removed FTC commissioners over policy

    In 1933, President Franklin Roosevelt removed FTC Commissioner William Humphrey, writing that their minds did not "go along together" on the commission's policies. The Supreme Court held in 1935 that the law allowed removal only for cause. In June 2026, ruling on President Trump's 2025 firing of Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter, the Court overruled that decision 6 to 3, so FTC commissioners can now be removed at will.

    United States (Federal Trade Commission) · 1933-2026 · Source: Supreme Court of the United States, Trump v. Slaughter, No. 25-332, 2026

    How it works
    Ending removal protection for commissioners narrows regulatory independence. The further claim, that at-will removal changes enforcement priorities, has no measured case yet.
    Evidence
    Documented for the legal change. In Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026), the Supreme Court held the FTC's for-cause removal protection unconstitutional and overruled what remained of Humphrey's Executor, leaving the Federal Reserve and non-Article III courts unresolved. In Trump v. Cook the same day, the Court left removal protection in place for a Federal Reserve governor. The Congressional Research Service explains the ruling's scope and open questions.
    Response
    Congress, agencies and the courts would protect statutory duties, require published reasons, keep records, protect professional case development and maintain congressional oversight, and would analyze the remaining tenure arrangements separately.
    Who acts
    Congress; agencies; courts
    Tradeoff
    Slaughter leaves Federal Reserve tenure and ordinary career-service protections undecided.
    Success looks like
    Enforcement reversals made without explanation, vacancies, and compliance with review.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-48 Agency independence after the Slaughter ruling. Builds independence from records, public reasons for removal and agency structure after Slaughter.
  • State-level rules can weaken democratic accountabilityIn the real world: Utah lawmakers replaced a voter-approved redistricting reformWell supportedX07

    Some state legislatures have drawn maps that protect supermajorities, taken over local boards and overridden city rules on labor and housing. These state choices decide how much accountability voters have, whatever happens in Washington.

    The problem, in the real world

    Utah lawmakers replaced a voter-approved redistricting reform

    In November 2018, Utah voters passed Proposition 4, creating an independent redistricting commission and barring maps that unduly favor a party. In 2020 the legislature repealed and replaced it, and in 2021 lawmakers adopted their own congressional map, splitting Salt Lake County four ways. In July 2024 the Utah Supreme Court held that such voter reforms are protected from unfettered legislative repeal.

    Utah · 2018-2024 · Source: Utah Supreme Court (via Justia), League of Women Voters of Utah v. Utah State Legislature, 2024 UT 21, 2024

    A fix, in the real world

    New York's top court struck a partisan congressional map

    In 2014, New York voters amended their constitution to create an independent redistricting commission and ban partisan gerrymandering. When the Democratic-controlled legislature passed its own congressional map in 2022, the Court of Appeals struck it down on April 27, finding it was drawn with impermissible partisan purpose. The court ordered a trial court working with a special master to adopt new maps.

    The legislature's map, which a lower court found would yield 22 Democratic-majority districts out of 26, was set aside in favor of court-adopted maps for 2022.

    New York · 2014-2022 · Source: New York Court of Appeals (New York State Law Reporting Bureau), Matter of Harkenrider v Hochul, 2022 NY Slip Op 02833, 38 NY3d 494, 2022

    How it works
    Gerrymanders that protect legislative supermajorities, state takeovers of local boards and preemption of local rules erode democratic quality in some states.
    Evidence
    Well supported. Grumbach's Laboratories Against Democracy (2022) builds a state democracy index and documents declines in some states, including supermajority gerrymanders and preemption of city labor and housing rules. Georgia's 2021 SB 202 authorizes the state to take over county election administration. The Congressional Research Service has documented the mid-decade congressional redraws of 2025 and 2026.
    Response
    State legislatures, state courts and voters by initiative would adopt enforceable districting criteria, limits on preemption and independent state election boards.
    Who acts
    Tradeoff
    A state that adopts neutral maps on its own can lose seats to states that do not, which invites retaliatory redraws.
    Success looks like
    Partisan bias in state maps, preemption laws enacted, and takeovers of local boards.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-04 Independent citizen commissions draw election maps. Independent commissions take map-drawing away from the supermajority the map would protect.
    • ReformR-45 Verifiable elections with paper records and audits. Sets a floor of lawful certification and protected officials that independent state election boards would carry out.
  • State supreme courts decide whether maps and voter-approved reforms take effectIn the real world: Virginia's top court voided a voter-approved map amendmentDocumentedX15

    In 2026 the supreme courts of Missouri, Virginia and Utah decided whether new congressional maps and voter-approved changes would take effect. Spending on state supreme court elections reached a record $157 million in 2023 and 2024.

    The problem, in the real world

    Virginia's top court voided a voter-approved map amendment

    On April 21, 2026, Virginia voters narrowly approved a Democratic-backed amendment allowing congressional districts to be redrawn mid-decade. On May 8, the Supreme Court of Virginia struck it down 4 to 3, ruling that lawmakers first passed it after voting had begun in the 2025 House of Delegates elections. The current maps stay in place for 2026.

    Virginia · 2026 · Source: Virginia Mercury, Supreme Court of Virginia strikes down redistricting amendment, keeps current maps in place, 2026

    A fix, in the real world

    Arizona voters kept retention elections for judges

    Arizona voters decide whether to keep appointed supreme court justices in retention elections. In 2024, 78% of them rejected an amendment to end those votes. The Brennan Center reports that retention races have drawn less spending than contested elections, though an Oklahoma justice lost one in 2024 after $3.6 million in group spending.

    Arizona kept its appointment-plus-retention system, which the Brennan Center finds draws less money than contested races, while warning that retention fights are getting costlier.

    Arizona · 2024 · Source: Brennan Center for Justice, The Politics of Judicial Elections 2023-24, 2026

    How it works
    State supreme courts now decide whether mid-decade congressional maps and voter-approved reforms take effect, as Missouri, Virginia and Utah show, while spending on those courts' own elections reached a record $157 million in 2023 and 2024.
    Evidence
    Documented. Missouri's Supreme Court upheld the 2025 mid-decade map 4 to 3 on March 24, 2026, then unanimously suspended it on September 3 until voters decide Proposition A on November 3, 2026. On September 10 the U.S. Supreme Court, with no public dissent, stayed a federal order that would have forced use of the new map, so Missouri votes in 2026 under its 2022 map. On May 8, 2026, the Supreme Court of Virginia ruled 4 to 3 that a redistricting amendment voters approved on April 21 was invalid because the legislature's first passage came after voting had begun in the 2025 House of Delegates elections. Utah's Supreme Court held in 2024 that the initiative power is constitutionally protected, and a trial judge imposed a court-selected map for 2026. The Brennan Center, an advocacy organization, counted $157.3 million spent on state supreme court elections in 2023 and 2024 across 79 seats in 35 states, a record, with interest groups outspending candidates for the first time.
    Response
    State legislatures and voters would require disclosure of spending in judicial elections and consider merit selection of justices followed by retention elections. State courts would be treated as a check on maps.
    Who acts
    Tradeoff
    Merit selection moves the choice of justices further from voters, and disclosure rules raise privacy concerns for small donors.
    Success looks like
    Share of judicial-election spending with an identified source.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-08 Disclose the original funders of political spending. Disclosure of original funders applies to spending in state supreme court elections.

News, records and public information 4

  • Local newsrooms close and fewer reporters watch local governmentIn the real world: Gallup, New Mexico, loses its paper after 62 yearsWell supportedI001

    When a local paper or station closes, fewer reporters attend council meetings, read budgets or question officials. Residents lose a shared source of facts about local decisions, and local officials face less public scrutiny.

    The problem, in the real world

    Gallup, New Mexico, loses its paper after 62 years

    In January 2026, the Gallup Independent in Gallup, New Mexico, printed its last issue after 62 years. Its circulation had fallen from 18,000 in 2006 to under 5,000. Bob Zollinger, whose family ran the paper, worries the city council and county commission will now meet with no reporter present.

    Gallup, New Mexico · 2026 · Source: Source NM, NM news desert grows with closure of longtime Gallup newspaper, 2026

    A fix, in the real world

    New Jersey funds local news through a state-created consortium

    New Jersey's 2018 law created the Civic Information Consortium, a nonprofit that funds local journalism with donations and state money. It has issued more than $12 million in grants. State support fell from $4 million in fiscal 2024 to $2.5 million in fiscal 2026, and Gov. Mikie Sherrill's first budget proposal would zero it out.

    Sen. Andrew Zwicker's bill would direct at least $5 million a year to the consortium but had not reached a committee vote, and the article cites no study of whether the grants brought closer scrutiny of officials.

    New Jersey · 2018-2026 · Source: New Jersey Monitor, Lawmakers eye funding stream for NJ PBS, local news, 2026

    How it works
    When local news outlets close, fewer reporters examine local government, and residents share less common knowledge about the decisions made in their name.
    Evidence
    Well supported. The 2025 State of Local News census counted 212 U.S. counties with no local news source (the report's landing page gives 213). A 2020 study by Gao, Lee and Murphy linked newspaper closures to higher borrowing costs for local governments. Hayes and Lawless (2021) found that shrinking local coverage goes with lower political engagement and knowledge; their panel and content data support associations, and the authors limit their causal claims.
    Response
    State legislatures and local philanthropies would create an independently governed local-news fund. It would pay formula grants, keep funders away from editorial decisions and publish data on every award.
    Who acts
    State legislatures; local philanthropies
    Tradeoff
    Public money can invite political control of coverage. The design keeps the people who appoint the fund's board separate from the people who make editorial decisions.
    Success looks like
    Counties with a local news source, reporters per resident, and the corrections that funded outlets publish.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-32 Public and philanthropic funding for local news. Pays reporters to cover local government with an editorial firewall, which is the fund this record proposes.
  • Chain owners cut local reportingIn the real world: Stations bought by Sinclair shift toward national politicsPlausibleI002

    When one company buys many local papers or stations, it often cuts local staff and shares content across its outlets. The strongest study, of one TV station owner, found coverage moved toward national politics and viewers left.

    The problem, in the real world

    Stations bought by Sinclair shift toward national politics

    In September 2017, Sinclair Broadcast Group finished buying 14 local TV stations from Bonten Media Group. A study in the American Political Science Review found the stations' coverage of national politics rose about 25% while local politics coverage fell. Their coverage also moved to the right, and a small drop in viewership was not statistically significant.

    Seven U.S. TV markets served by former Bonten stations · 2017 · Source: American Political Science Review (Martin and McCrain), Local News and National Politics, 2019

    A fix, in the real world

    Regulators' review stops Sinclair's bid for Tribune Media

    In July 2018, the Federal Communications Commission sent Sinclair's $3.9 billion bid for Tribune Media to a hearing before a judge. Commissioners questioned whether planned sales of stations to buyers close to Sinclair were a sham that would let Sinclair keep running them. Tribune walked away from the deal in August.

    The merger collapsed, Sinclair said it had not misled the commission, and no study has measured what the outcome meant for local coverage.

    United States · 2018 · Source: CNN Business, CNN Money report on Tribune ending the Sinclair merger (lede: 'The Sinclair Broadcast Group acquisition of Tribune Media is dead.'), 2018

    How it works
    Chains that buy local outlets often cut local reporting staff. One strong study found that one owner, Sinclair Broadcast Group, shifted its acquired stations toward national political coverage; whether common owners in general centralize the news agenda is untested.
    Evidence
    Plausible. Martin and McCrain (2019, American Political Science Review) found that local TV stations bought by Sinclair shifted toward national and right-leaning political coverage and lost viewers. The study covers one ownership group. Staff cuts at chain-owned outlets appear in industry counts such as the 2025 State of Local News report.
    Response
    Congress, the Federal Communications Commission and the federal antitrust agencies would review local news mergers for their effect on competition and on the number of independent outlets. Owners would disclose who ultimately owns each outlet and how many newsroom staff it employs.
    Who acts
    Congress; FCC; antitrust agencies
    Tradeoff
    Owning many outlets proves neither biased coverage nor illegal market power, so each deal needs its own evidence.
    Success looks like
    More distinct owners in each local market and more original local reporting.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-32 Public and philanthropic funding for local news. Funds independent local reporters, which offsets the staff cuts that follow acquisitions; ownership itself stays unchanged.
  • Platforms take the advertising that once paid for reportingIn the real world: Judge finds Google illegally dominated online ad toolsWell supportedI003

    Most of the advertising money that used to support newspapers now goes to large online platforms. News organizations still pay the cost of reporting, so they cover fewer public decisions.

    The problem, in the real world

    Judge finds Google illegally dominated online ad tools

    In April 2025, a federal judge in Virginia ruled that Google held an illegal monopoly over some of the technology websites use to sell ads. Publishers pay a 20% fee on Google's ad exchange. In September 2026 the judge ordered six years of rule changes and declined to force a sale, and Google said it would appeal.

    United States (federal court in Alexandria, Virginia) · 2025-2026 · Source: Reuters (republished by The Star), Google should relax ad tech rules, appoint antitrust monitor, US judge finds, 2026

    A fix, in the real world

    Canada tried a tax credit for news subscriptions

    Canada let taxpayers claim a credit worth 15% of up to $500 spent on qualifying digital news subscriptions. About 302,000 people filed for it in 2020, roughly 1% of the country's more than 27 million tax filers, and the average credit was $36.

    Uptake was about 1% in the first year, and the article reports no measured effect on subscriptions; one publisher called the result negligible.

    Canada · 2020 · Source: Nieman Lab, Canada offered a tax credit to encourage digital news subscriptions. Here's how it's going, 2022

    How it works
    Large online platforms now collect most of the advertising money that once paid for news, while publishers still carry the cost of reporting.
    Evidence
    Well supported. Industry estimates compiled by the Pew Research Center show U.S. newspaper advertising revenue falling from about $49 billion in 2005 to under $10 billion in 2022. The 2025 State of Local News census counted 212 counties with no local news source.
    Response
    A state legislature would pilot reader vouchers and refundable tax credits for local news subscriptions. Nonprofit and small independent outlets would qualify alongside established publishers.
    Who acts
    State legislature
    Tradeoff
    Subsidies can flow mostly to large, established publishers. Eligibility rules need to be neutral about viewpoint and simple enough for small outlets to use.
    Success looks like
    New subscribers, readers reached in places with little coverage, and public cost per reader.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-32 Public and philanthropic funding for local news. Replaces part of the lost advertising money with public and philanthropic funding behind an editorial firewall.
    • ReformR-44 Competition remedies for search and ad markets. Opens search and ad-tech markets so a smaller share of advertising money is captured by a few platforms.
  • Public records arrive too late to be usefulIn the real world: Federal records backlog jumps by a third in 2024DocumentedI013

    Federal agencies take weeks or months to answer requests for public records, and backlogs keep growing. Slow answers stall investigations by reporters and residents.

    The problem, in the real world

    Federal records backlog jumps by a third in 2024

    In fiscal 2024, the backlog of overdue federal Freedom of Information Act requests grew 33%, to 267,056, by the Brechner Center's count of federal data. Simple requests took 44 days on average, up from 39 the year before. Agencies spent an estimated $723 million processing requests.

    United States (federal agencies) · 2024 · Source: Brechner Center for Freedom of Information, University of Florida, FOIA requests, denials, backlogs, delays, costs surge in FY 2024, 2025

    How it works
    Slow responses to public-records requests obstruct investigations. The claim that delay favors people with inside access is an inference the sources do not test.
    Evidence
    Documented. The Justice Department reported 1.50 million federal Freedom of Information Act requests in fiscal year 2024, up 25%, with simple requests taking 44 days on average, the longest since 2011. A tabulation of FOIA.gov data by the Brechner Center counted a year-end backlog of 267,056 requests, up 33%, and a record-low 12% of requests granted in full.
    Response
    Congress, federal agencies and the states would fund records officers, publish records openly in machine-readable form and enforce response deadlines with an appeal that works.
    Who acts
    Congress; agencies; states
    Tradeoff
    Redactions still have to protect privacy and legitimate security interests.
    Success looks like
    Age of the request backlog, and how complete agencies' proactive publication is.

Money, lobbying and influence 1

  • Court rulings limit what campaign-finance laws can doIn the real world: Supreme Court struck down overall caps on givingDocumentedI048

    Supreme Court rulings under the First Amendment have struck down many limits on political spending and contributions. Disclosure and public financing remain legal options, while broader limits would need a constitutional amendment.

    The problem, in the real world

    Supreme Court struck down overall caps on giving

    In 2014, the Supreme Court struck down federal caps on the total one person could give to candidates and political committees combined in a two-year cycle. Alabama resident Shaun McCutcheon and the Republican National Committee had challenged the 2012 cap of $117,000. The 5 to 4 ruling found the caps did not serve the only government interest the Court had accepted.

    U.S. Supreme Court · 2014 · Source: Federal Election Commission, McCutcheon, et al. v. FEC, 2014

    A fix, in the real world

    New York State's match raised the share from small donors

    New York State began matching small donations to legislative candidates in 2024, matching the first $50 of a constituent's gift 12 to 1. In the first cycle, 328 candidates took part. A Brennan Center study found that small gifts plus matching funds made up 45% of campaign money, up from 5% in earlier cycles.

    In-district small donors doubled to about 50,800, and the share of money from large donors and organizations fell from 72% in 2022 to 38% in 2024.

    New York · 2024 · Source: Sludge, New York Used a New Public Campaign Financing Program in 2024. How Did It Work?, 2025

    How it works
    Current First Amendment doctrine blocks many proposed limits on political money.
    Evidence
    Documented. Citizens United v. FEC (2010) allowed unlimited independent spending by corporations and unions and upheld disclosure. McCutcheon v. FEC (2014) struck down aggregate contribution limits and held that only quid pro quo corruption or its appearance justifies limits. NRSC v. FEC (June 30, 2026) struck down limits on party spending coordinated with candidates.
    Response
    Congress and the states would pursue disclosure and public financing now, and separately draft a constitutional amendment authorizing reasonable limits on political money with safeguards for speech.
    Who acts
    Congress; states
    Tradeoff
    Amendments are hard to pass, and vague language could give officials power to censor.
    Success looks like
    A route to enactment, review for effects on rights, and durable compliance.

    Reforms aimed at it

    • ReformR-07 Public matching for small donations and vouchers. Public financing is one of the tools current doctrine allows.
    • ReformR-08 Disclose the original funders of political spending. Disclosure survived Citizens United and is the other tool current doctrine allows.

Congress, agencies and public services 1

  • Small local governments lack money and expert staffIn the real world: Thousands of rural communities lack staff to seek aidPlausibleI165

    Towns with a small tax base often cannot afford the lawyers, engineers or procurement specialists their duties require. State grants and shared regional services are proposed ways to fill the gap.

    The problem, in the real world

    Thousands of rural communities lack staff to seek aid

    Headwaters Economics, an independent research group, counts 7,886 U.S. communities with very limited capacity, judged by measures such as local government staff and expertise. Its 2026 index finds 46% of them face high flood risk, and it warns that many lack the staff and tax base to apply for federal programs.

    United States (rural communities) · 2026 · Source: Headwaters Economics, Rural Capacity Index, 2026

    How it works
    Small governments lack the tax base and the legal and procurement capacity their duties require.
    Evidence
    Plausible. Government Accountability Office simulations show persistent operating gaps in state and local budgets; they do not measure staff capacity directly.
    Response
    States and local governments, with federal grants from Congress, would provide equalizing grants, shared professional services and regional technical help, with public accountability for results.
    Who acts
    States; local governments; Congress for grants
    Tradeoff
    Shared services can make government less responsive to each town, and recurring costs need steady funding.
    Success looks like
    Services completed, fiscal stress, and staffing gaps.

Loop R10 · Safe-seat loop · Reinforcing, feeds itself

Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates

Read it aloud More safe seats, more seats settled in the primary, less risk of losing office, more incumbents control election rules, and back to more safe seats.

You are here

In a safe seat, the primary decides who wins, and few people vote in it. With little threat in November, officeholders answer to that smaller electorate and face less pressure from the wider public. Officials who cannot easily be removed can then write election rules that keep seats safe.

Point at, tap or tab to a box or a step to read it.

Red marks where reform R-01, All-party primaries, acts: on L25, L08, C2. Select another reform to move the red to its targets.

Walk the loop

Start at C1, Safe seats, and suppose it rises. Press Play, or Next step to follow one numbered connection at a time.

  1. L08, Safe seats make the primary decisive. More safe seats means more seats settled in the primary. Sign +, raises; documented; under 2 years.
  2. L25, Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure. More seats settled in the primary means less risk of losing office. Sign −, lowers; well supported; under 2 years.
  3. L53, Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves. Less risk of losing office means more incumbents control election rules. Sign −, lowers; plausible; 2 to 10 years.
  4. L42, Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats. More incumbents control election rules means more safe seats. Sign +, raises; documented; 2 to 10 years.

Step by step

  1. Step 1 ConnectionL08

    Safe seats make the primary decisive

    When one party is sure to win the general election, the real choice happens in that party's primary.

    + raises · Documented: on the public record · under 2 years

    Keep in mind Unite America, a reform advocacy group, counted 88% of House seats (383 of 435) as effectively decided in the 2026 primaries using Cook Political Report ratings; the count depends on the group's own definition of a decided seat.

  2. Step 2 ConnectionL25

    Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure

    When the primary decides the seat, the November election poses little threat, and incumbents answer mainly to the smaller group that votes in primaries.

    − lowers · Well supported: strong research evidence · under 2 years

    Keep in mind Incumbents can still lose primaries; this link measures the loss of general-election pressure, and total pressure depends on how often primaries are contested.

  3. Step 3 ConnectionL53 The weakest step

    Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves

    Officeholders who face little risk of losing can redraw maps and change election rules to protect their position.

    − lowers · Plausible: some evidence · 2 to 10 years

    Keep in mind The evidence is events, chiefly the 2025 mid-decade redistricting in states with one-party control, and legal analysis (Hasen 2020); no study measures this link directly.

  4. Step 4 ConnectionL42

    Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats

    Officeholders who draw district lines can pack or split voters to make their seats safer, and redrawing between censuses repeats the effect sooner.

    + raises · Documented: on the public record · 2 to 10 years

    Keep in mind Residential sorting also produces safe seats without any map drawing (Chen and Rodden 2013), so the count of safe seats has more than one cause.

The evidence

L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive and L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats are documented, and L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure is well supported. The weakest step is L53: Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves, graded plausible: its evidence is the 2025 mid-decade redistricting in states with one-party control and legal analysis. Whether primaries make legislators more extreme is a separate, contested question, and the strongest tests found no effect.

Keep in mind

Seat safety also comes from where voters live, and the claim that primary reform makes legislators more moderate is contested, so the loop concerns accountability more than ideology.

In the real world

Alaska's top-four primary with ranked-choice general elections survived a 2024 repeal measure by 743 votes out of 321,203 after a December 2024 recount. A second repeal is on the November 3, 2026 ballot, combined with repeal of the state's rule requiring disclosure of the true source of political donations. One election cycle is too short to show the design's long-run effect on accountability.

Where it is heading

Running up, 2 to 10 years a turn. Measured by: Share of House seats settled in primaries, 2012 to 2024.

Improvement or decline can reinforce itself.

Reform R-01 · Rules · All-party primaries

All-party primaries with ranked general elections

Every voter, whatever their party, could vote in one first-round election, and two or more candidates would advance to a November ballot that all voters use. In seats that one party usually wins, the choice now made in a low-turnout party primary would move to the full electorate. In Massachusetts, unenrolled voters already pick one party's ballot. Under Question 3, every voter would see all candidates on one primary ballot from 2028. The Atlas takes no position on Question 3 or Ballot Measure 2.

Where it acts

The problem it answers

Cook Political Report rated 398 of 435 House seats safe for 2026, as reported by Unite America, an advocacy organization that funds primary-reform campaigns. Unite America's own count puts 383 seats (88%) as effectively decided in the 2026 primaries, which drew about 22.7 million voters, 9.4% of eligible voters. Both counts rest on ratings, which are forecasts, and on the group's definition of a safe seat.

  • Closed primaries shut unaffiliated voters out of the deciding election

    In a closed primary only voters enrolled in a party can help choose its nominee. Where the primary effectively decides the seat, unaffiliated voters have no say in the contest that settles it.

  • In safe seats, a small primary electorate picks the winner

    In most House districts one party is sure to win in November, so its primary decides who takes office. Turnout in those primaries is a small fraction of eligible voters.

What it changes

In a safe seat the general election is predictable, so the party primary picks the winner (L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive). That weakens the threat incumbents face from the wider public (L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure). An all-party primary sends more than one candidate to November, which aims to lower C2: How often the primary decides the winner and raise C3: Risk of losing office. A top-two design advances two candidates; a top-four design advances four and can be paired with a ranked-choice general election. The reform sits on loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates), loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance) and loop R11 (Party loyalty weakens consequences for breaking norms).

Where it acts

On the safe-seat loop, R-01 aims at L25, L08, C2, marked in red. It also sits on loops B4 and R11.

Point at, tap or tab to a box or a step to read it.

Likely effects, family by family

Each family is rated on its own and never added to the others. Confidence: medium (participation); low (moderation).

−M−S0+S+M+L
  • Democratic qualityModerate positive
  • Government efficacySmall positive
  • Economic performanceNo expected effect
  • Income and wealth equalityNo expected effect

Routes to adoption

States set nomination rules for state and federal offices. Where a state allows citizen initiatives, voters can change those rules at the ballot box, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; Massachusetts Question 3 and Alaska's repeal measure are both on the November 3, 2026 ballot. Legislatures can act by statute, rated low because legislators elected under the current rules rarely change them. Home-rule cities can adopt the approach for municipal offices (medium) unless state law bans ranked ballots. Congress could act for federal races under the Elections Clause of the Constitution, which gets the lowest feasibility rating because most bills need 60 Senate votes while the filibuster stands (R-12).

The evidence, graded twice

Problem evidence

Plausible: some evidence

Cook Political Report rated 398 of 435 House seats safe for 2026, as reported by Unite America, an advocacy organization that funds primary-reform campaigns. Unite America's own count puts 383 seats (88%) as effectively decided in the 2026 primaries, which drew about 22.7 million voters, 9.4% of eligible voters. Both counts rest on ratings, which are forecasts, and on the group's definition of a safe seat.

Remedy evidence

Contested: evidence disputed

More contested general elections and more candidates entering races are plausible results. Whether legislators become more moderate is contested: a 2014 study of state legislators by McGhee and colleagues found that more open primaries had little consistent effect on ideology, and experimental work finds that primary effects depend on conditions. Main limitation: Alaska's top-four system has a short record, so there is no long-run U.S. test of a top-four primary paired with a ranked general election.

Tradeoffs

Parties lose control over who carries their label, and some voters lose a party ballot line they value. Ranked tabulation takes longer to count. When two candidates from the same party advance, voters from the other party have no nominee of their own in November.

How it could fail

Party organizations in both major parties and incumbents secure in their primaries are expected to resist. Parties can coordinate so that only one of their candidates competes; in Alaska in 2024 one candidate withdrew after the top-four primary, with party consultants citing the risk of splitting the vote. Voters or legislatures can reverse the rule, and nineteen states ban ranked-choice voting in some or all elections. The reform can also fall short if turnout stays low in the deciding round, or if voters misread the ballot and trust in results drops.

Status

As of October 15, 2026, two measures on the November 3, 2026 ballot would change how primaries work. Alaska's Ballot Measure 2 (petition 24ESEG) would repeal the state's top-four primary and ranked-choice general election and return to party primaries. Massachusetts voters decide Question 3, which would replace party primaries for state and congressional offices with one primary listing every candidate, the top two advancing to November; if approved, it takes effect January 1, 2028. Nineteen states prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, by the National Conference of State Legislatures' count.

Checked October 15, 2026.

Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign for Massachusetts Question 3 and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead. He also co-leads Ranked Choice Melrose, a local campaign.

How to read the atlas · the shared language

Every line says what happens next, and how sure we are.

Five habits carry through every drawing in the atlas. Learn them once here and they hold on every floor, loop and reform.

1

The tip is the effect

Every arrow ends at what changes. The tag on the line says which way.

  • Plus, raises. The connected variables tend to move in the same direction, with the model's other conditions held steady. A positive sign does not mean a benefit.

  • Minus, lowers. The connected variables tend to move in opposite directions, with the model's other conditions held steady.

  • Open diamond, decides. A connection showing that one body holds legal power over something: it appoints, appropriates, preempts, enforces or sets a rate. It says who decides, without saying which way the decision goes, so it has no sign and never closes a loop.

2

Texture is the evidence

Solid lines rest on the record or on strong research. Broken lines carry less. The pattern stays the same at every weight and survives a black and white print.

  • Documented, on the public record. The confidence label for a fact or event on the public record: a statute, a court ruling or an official statistic.

  • Well supported, strong research evidence. The confidence label for a relationship on which several credible studies, designed to rule out other explanations, agree about direction.

  • Plausible, some evidence. The confidence label for a coherent mechanism with some supporting evidence, where the studies are weak or few.

  • Contested, evidence disputed. The confidence label for a relationship on which credible studies disagree.

  • Hypothesis, untested. The confidence label for a proposed relationship that needs stronger evidence.

  • Conceptual step, an open line: a step in a sketched loop with no numbered connection.

3

Ticks count the wait

The time between a change and its effect. Codes: S, under 2 years; M, 2 to 10 years; L, over 10 years.

  • Under 2 years. One tick.

  • 2 to 10 years. Two ticks.

  • Over 10 years. Three ticks.

4

Loops have a character

A chain of causes that returns to its starting variable. Reinforcing loops amplify change and balancing loops counteract it; either kind can produce good or harmful results.

5

Color is the layer

The ground under a floor says which layer of the model it belongs to. Red marks one thing per view: where a reform acts, or the item you selected.

White floors

The core of the model: Wealth, Voice, Elections, Checks and Policy, with outside forces beside them.

Newsprint, below the ground line

Your household and Technology: the economy and technology layers the core stands on.

?

Common mix-ups

Questions readers get wrong, with the atlas’s answer.

  • A district where the incumbent could lose but never does: is that pressure, sanction, both or neither?

    Pressure without sanction. Risk of losing office can be present while incumbents defeated stays at zero; the accountability loop needs both.

    The common mistake Treating any competitive-looking seat as accountable.

  • In one or two sentences, explain how a zoning meeting can change rents across a city.

    Owners whose equity rises with scarcity attend and block new homes; fewer homes keep rents high.

    The common mistake Rents rise only because landlords are greedy, or only because of interest rates.

  • Does housing scarcity raise the top 1% share of wealth?

    Not in the atlas. Scarcity widens the owner-renter gap; when house prices outrun stocks the top 1% share tends to fall.

    The common mistake Equating every wealth gap with the top 1%.

  • The 43-day shutdown happened. What part of the trust-through-service loop does that prove?

    That service failed (an event on quality of public services). It does not show that the failure lowered trust, or that trust lowered funding; those links carry their own grades.

    The common mistake A vivid case proves a whole loop.

  • Where does a rule allowing homes by right enter the atlas?

    At the link “Owners' equity drives opposition to new housing”, where owners with equity resist new homes, and at housing scarcity.

    The common mistake Reforms act on outcomes directly.

  • Name one reform a state can adopt without Congress, and one that needs sixty Senate votes today.

    Examples: on-cycle local elections (state statute); proportional House districts (federal statute).

    The common mistake Every reform waits on Washington.

  • A line labelled auth, with no plus or minus sign, connects Congress to public investment. What does it mean?

    Authority: Congress has the power to decide; the line does not say which way it will.

    The common mistake Every line is a cause.

  • Why does the atlas not give each reform a single score?

    The four outcome families use different units, some reforms help one and cost another, and the evidence differs in quality.

    The common mistake More plus signs means a better reform.

  • What did the largest feed experiments find about polarization?

    Changing the feed changed what people saw a great deal and their partisan hostility little or not at all.

    The common mistake Algorithms caused polarization, settled.

  • Household income rose last year. Does that mean household wealth rose too?

    Not necessarily. Income is a flow; wealth is a stock that also moves with asset prices and debts.

    The common mistake Stock-flow confusion (Sweeney and Sterman).

  • The same house-price rise: who gains most, a renter under 35 or an owner over 55?

    The owner; ownership and equity differ sharply by age.

    The common mistake Averages describe every household.

  • Pick one reform profile. Which office decides it, and how could you reach that office?

    It depends on the route. The route board on this page lists who acts on each route for every profile.

    The common mistake No one decides; it just happens.

  • Name one thing that decides how a productivity gain is split between pay and profit.

    Bargaining power, which the rules for organizing shape. Productivity growth raises what can be paid; it does not settle who gets it.

    The common mistake Pay tracks productivity automatically, or pay never responds to it.

  • Which office sets your electric rates?

    For an investor-owned utility, the state public utility commission. For public power or a co-op, a city council or co-op board. In PJM states the grid operator's capacity auction, overseen by federal regulators, also feeds into bills.

    The common mistake The power company sets its own prices, or Washington sets them.

A

Terms

Variable
A quantity or condition in the model that can rise or fall. Its definition states what a higher or lower value means.
Connection
A claimed relationship between two variables. Its record explains the mechanism, gives the evidence grade and states the delay. Connection IDs begin with L, LE, LT, LX or T.
Feedback loop
A chain of causes that returns to its starting variable. Reinforcing loops amplify change and balancing loops counteract it; either kind can produce good or harmful results.
Reinforcing loop (R)
A feedback loop whose returning effect amplifies the first change. Improvement or decline can reinforce itself.
Balancing loop (B)
A feedback loop whose response pushes back against the first change. How well it works depends on whether each corrective step can act.
Delay
The time between a change and its effect. Codes: S, under 2 years; M, 2 to 10 years; L, over 10 years.
Documented
The confidence label for a fact or event on the public record: a statute, a court ruling or an official statistic. It establishes the event; it says nothing about the size of an effect unless the record does.
Well-supported
The confidence label for a relationship on which several credible studies, designed to rule out other explanations, agree about direction. Each study's setting and limits still apply.
Plausible
The confidence label for a coherent mechanism with some supporting evidence, where the studies are weak or few.
Contested
The confidence label for a relationship on which credible studies disagree. Both sides are shown with the connection.
Hypothesis
The confidence label for a proposed relationship that needs stronger evidence. Diagrams draw it as a dotted line, and it never serves as the only support for a claim.
Authority connection
A connection showing that one body holds legal power over something: it appoints, appropriates, preempts, enforces or sets a rate. It says who decides, without saying which way the decision goes, so it has no sign and never closes a loop.
Outside driver
A force that affects the model but whose own causes lie outside its boundary, such as technology, population patterns, trade, foreign interference and major shocks. Drawn as a rounded pill outside the clusters.
Issue record
One of 193 records beneath the map, with IDs such as I017 or X01. Each describes a documented problem, case or policy, names its mechanism, gives an evidence grade, status and sources, and links to a variable or connection where it can.
Reform profile
One of 50 entries, R-01 to R-50, describing a proposed change: the connections it aims at, the routes it can travel, what it depends on, separate evidence about the problem and the remedy, expected directions for each outcome family, and how it could fail.
Outcome family
One of four groups of results used to judge reforms: democratic quality, government efficacy, economic performance, and income and wealth equality. The families use different units and are never added together.
Feasibility
A judgment of whether a route to change is open under present political and legal conditions. The Atlas rates it high, medium, low or very low for 2026 to 2030.
Route
A path a reform can travel through government or civil society, such as a city ordinance, a state statute, a ballot measure, a federal statute, executive action, a court ruling or a constitutional amendment. The Atlas uses eleven routes.
Pathway
A guided answer to one everyday question, such as why rent went up. It gives a short answer, the main mechanisms, narrower questions, the offices that decide, possible responses and the evidence behind each claim.
Entry document
An ordinary paper a reader already handles, such as a rent renewal, a pay stub, a primary ballot, a bill or a notice, used as a starting point into the map.
Snapshot
The dated state of the research behind the Atlas, most recently October 15, 2026. Facts that were checked carry their own check date; inclusion in the snapshot alone does not mean a fact was rechecked on that date.

Who Do They Answer To? Systems Atlas V7, snapshot October 15, 2026. 51 variables, 118 connections, 23 loops, 50 reforms.
